# Robustness of the Test for Overreporting {#sec-app-test-robustness}

@tbl-evasion-test reports the sharp version of the test, which takes $\ln\hat\beta$ from corporations as the true value. This appendix reports two alternatives and shows that the test does not depend on the functional forms of the detection probability, the cost of evasion or the technology (@sec-app-test-general). @tbl-evasion-test-conservative gives the conservative test, which gives no credit for the corporations' moment. @tbl-evasion-test-bootstrap gives a bootstrap test that re-estimates $\ln\hat\beta$ in every replication and thereby carries the sampling error of the first stage.

## The test under general detection, cost and technology {#sec-app-test-general}

This section derives the results stated in @sec-testing-test: the test depends neither on the functional forms of the detection probability and the cost of evasion, nor on the Cobb-Douglas form of the technology.

**Setup.** Let output be $Y_{it}=G(K_{it},L_{it},M_{it})\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})$, with $G_M>0$, common to corporations and unincorporated firms in an industry. Let the detection probability and the cost of evasion depend on overreporting and on any other variables $Z_{it}$, possibly including materials: $q(e,Z)$ and $\kappa(e,Z)$. With $\mathbb{E}[\exp(\varepsilon_{it})]=1$ as in @sec-model, the part of expected profit that depends on materials and overreporting is

$$
(1-\tau_S)P_tG(K_{it},L_{it},M_{it})\exp(\omega_{it})-(1-\tau_P)\rho_tM_{it}+\tau_P\rho_te_{it}\big[1-(1+\phi)q(e_{it},Z_{it})\big]-\kappa(e_{it},Z_{it}).
$$

**Under the null.** A truthful firm faces no detection and incurs no cost of evasion: $q(0,Z)=0$ and $\kappa(0,Z)=0$ for every $Z$. At $e_{it}=0$, the evasion terms are zero for every $M_{it}$, and so are their derivatives with respect to $M_{it}$. The materials condition is the one without evasion, $(1-\tau_S)P_tG_M\exp(\omega_{it})=(1-\tau_P)\rho_t$. Multiplying by $M_{it}$ and dividing by measured output gives

$$
\ln\left(\frac{(1-\tau_P)\rho_tM_{it}}{(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}}\right)=\ln D(K_{it},L_{it},M_{it})-\varepsilon_{it},\qquad D\equiv\frac{G_M M}{G},
$$ {#eq-app-share-general}

where $D$ is the output elasticity of materials. Under Cobb-Douglas, $D=\beta$ and @eq-app-share-general is @eq-share-net. Corporations identify $D$ as a function of inputs, $\ln D(K,L,M)=\mathbb{E}[s_{it}\mid K,L,M,\text{corporation}]$, provided measurement error is also independent of capital and labour.

**The residual.** Evaluating the elasticity at each firm's reported materials, and adding and subtracting the log share of true materials, gives, suppressing $K_{it}$ and $L_{it}$,

$$
\mathcal V_{it}\equiv s_{it}-\ln D(M^*_{it})=\ln\left(\frac{M^*_{it}}{M_{it}}\right)-\ln\left(\frac{D(M^*_{it})}{D(M_{it})}\right)-\varepsilon_{it}=\ln\left(\frac{H(M^*_{it})}{H(M_{it})}\right)-\varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-app-residual-general}

where $H\equiv G/G_M$. Under the null, $M^*_{it}=M_{it}$ and $\mathcal V_{it}=-\varepsilon_{it}$ for any $G$. The test's size does not depend on the technology, and a rejection means that some firms overreport. Under the alternative, $M^*_{it}>M_{it}$ for overreporting firms, and $\ln\big(H(M^*_{it})/H(M_{it})\big)$ is positive whenever $H$ increases in materials. Since $\partial H/\partial M=1-GG_{MM}/G_M^2$, this holds when output is concave in materials, $G_{MM}\le0$. The exact condition is weaker: $GG_{MM}<G_M^2$, i.e. $\ln G$ concave in materials. The expected residual is then positive and the test stays one-sided. Under Cobb-Douglas, $H=M/\beta$ and $\ln\big(H(M^*_{it})/H(M_{it})\big)=u_{it}$, as in @eq-ob-ev.

If $q$ or $\kappa$ depend on materials, evaders' true materials may depart from @eq-app-share-general under the alternative. This changes the power of the test, not its size: under the null no firm evades.

**A second flexible input.** Let $N_{it}$ be a second flexible input that is not creditable against the sales tax, such as energy, fuels or services. Under the model, the firm gains nothing by overreporting it and reports it truthfully. With $N_{it}$ in the technology, $G(K_{it},L_{it},M_{it},N_{it})$, its log share, $s^N_{it}\equiv\ln\big(P_{N,t}N_{it}/(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}\big)$, satisfies $s^N_{it}=\ln D_N-\varepsilon_{it}$, with $D_N\equiv G_NN/G$. Evaluating $D_N$ at reported materials,

$$
\mathcal V^N_{it}\equiv s^N_{it}-\ln D_N(M^*_{it})=-\ln\left(\frac{D_N(M^*_{it})}{D_N(M_{it})}\right)-\varepsilon_{it}.
$$

Under the null, $\mathcal V^N_{it}=-\varepsilon_{it}$. Under the alternative, the first term differs from zero as long as $D_N$ is strictly monotone in materials; concavity is no longer needed. Its sign depends on the technology: negative if $D_N$ increases in materials, positive if it decreases. This version is a two-sided test, and a rejection still points only to overreporting.

**Estimation.** Beyond Cobb-Douglas, the elasticity varies with inputs. Estimating it from corporations and evaluating it at unincorporated firms' inputs requires a parametric form, such as translog, or overlap in inputs between the two groups; corporations are much larger. The test in @sec-testing is the Cobb-Douglas case, $D=\beta$.
